blocks.text: **The problem.** Given two arrays `a` and `b`, each sorted in ascending order, return their **union**: every **distinct** value that appears in either array, in sorted order.

blocks.alt: a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and b = [1, 2, 3, 6, 7]. Their union is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]; the shared values 1, 2 and 3 appear only once.

blocks.text: The union is like combining two guest lists: everyone invited by either host, but each person listed **once**. Duplicates can come from both directions — a value can repeat **inside** one array, and it can appear in **both** arrays.
Brute force: a set, then sort
Short and correct, but it spends **O((n + m) log(n + m))** sorting data that was already sorted, plus O(n + m) space for the set.
The key insight: merge, skipping repeats

Do exactly what **Merge two sorted arrays** does — always take the smaller front — but before appending a value, check it against the **last value appended**. Because values come out in sorted order, any duplicate is guaranteed to be sitting right next to its twin, so that single comparison catches every repeat.

blocks.alt: Merging a = [1, 1, 2, 3] and b = [2, 3, 3, 4] in sorted order gives 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4. Each value that equals the previous one is skipped, leaving [1, 2, 3, 4].

elements.text: a grey value equals the one before it → skip
elements.originalText: a grey value equals the one before it → skip

blocks.text: The loop keeps running while **either** array has values left; the first condition picks from `a` whenever `b` is used up, and from the smaller front otherwise. (In C++, `union` is a reserved word, so the function is called `unionOf`.)

blocks.alt: Set then sort: O((n+m) log(n+m)) time. Merge while skipping repeats: O(n+m) time. Both need O(n+m) space for the answer.

blocks.text: Each element is looked at once: **O(n + m) time**. The answer itself can hold up to n + m values.

items: **Identical arrays** — the union is one copy of the distinct values.
**One array empty** — the union is the other array without its repeats.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

Union, intersection and difference of sorted lists are the building blocks of search engines (combining the lists of pages that contain each word) and database joins. All three are "walk both lists together" with a different rule for what to keep.
